note: Every term a newcomer to Singapore's government would not know, and where the game introduces it. The game does not load this file. test/jargon.js plays careers and checks that each term's first appearance in a career is at one of its entry points: a card whose story makes the meaning clear, a line from game.json or rival.json that explains the term itself, or "start" (the start screen), "header" (rank, grade and ministry) or "engine:<kind>" (a line the engine writes, such as the pay line). After its entry point a term may be used freely. `meaning` is for writers and never appears in the game. `match` is a JavaScript regular expression for the term's uses; `examples` must match it and `skip` must not.

terms.meaning: Currently Estimated Potential: HR's private estimate of the highest grade an officer will ever reach, set early in a career and never told to the officer.
The yearly meeting where senior officers rank officers of the same grade against each other; only those near the top are promoted.
The yearly performance grade (A, B+, B, C or D) that decides promotion, written by your reporting officer.
Your direct boss in the service: the person who sets your work and writes your appraisal.
The service's salary grades: MX13 at the bottom up to MX9, then Superscale and Staff Grade; MR4 to MR1 for ministers. Shown beside your title.
A short internal memo that sets out a problem and asks the people above for a decision.
A government agency set up by its own Act of Parliament and run at arm's length from its ministry, such as HDB.
A security marking: the document is for the officers it is addressed to, and nobody else.
A high security classification; reading such a document needs clearance at that level.
The office that logs, stores and tracks every classified document in a building.
A committee of officials from several ministries, set up to settle a question none of them can settle alone.
The officers who write a committee's papers and minutes and do its work between meetings.
The Public Service Commission: awards government scholarships, holds the scholar's bond, and appoints senior officers.
The years a government scholar must serve in return for the scholarship; leaving early means paying damages.
People, usually family, who sign a scholar's bond deed and promise to pay if the scholar breaks it.
In the service, an officer who studied on a government scholarship and is expected to rise fast.
Dinner-and-dance: a division's yearly party, with a theme, a band and a lucky draw.
The Chinese New Year custom of tossing a raw-fish salad (yusheng) as high as possible while shouting good wishes.
The seventh month of the lunar calendar, when the spirits of the dead are said to roam.
State honours announced each National Day; pingat is Malay for medal.
The government's job portal, through which most officers apply.
The official word-for-word record of everything said in Parliament.
The part of a sitting when Members put questions to ministers; the questions, filed in advance, are Parliamentary Questions.
A follow-up question a Member may ask straight after a minister's answer, without notice.
Parliament, as its Members call it.
The party's officer in Parliament who makes sure its Members attend and vote as the party decides.
When the Prime Minister moves ministers and office holders between jobs.
An MP's weekly evening session where residents bring their problems and volunteers write appeal letters for them.
Group Representation Constituency: a large ward where voters elect a team of MPs, usually five, together.
Single Member Constituency: a ward that elects one MP, who runs alone.
To run in an election as a candidate.
terms.match: \b(?:[Ss]tand|[Ss]tands|[Ss]tanding|[Ss]tood)\b(?= (?:again|once more|one more time|for (?:Parliament|election|a seat)|at (?:the|this) (?:same |next |first )?(?:general )?election|in (?:a |the )?(?:GRC|single seat|election)|with the GRC team|alone in a single seat))|\bto stand\b(?=[.,;:])
examples: resigned from the service to stand, and
stood at the same general election
skip: Go, and stand at the back.
You stand on a campaign lorry
thick enough to stand up by itself

terms.meaning: The governing party's first, informal approach to someone it may field at an election: an invitation to tea.
skip: does not speak to you at the tea break

terms.meaning: A candidate's or MP's walk through a market, hawker centre or estate, meeting voters.
The day candidates file their papers to stand at an election; the campaign starts then.
The day before polling, when campaigning is banned.
An early count of a sample of votes, published on election night before the full result.
The weeks of Budget debate when Parliament goes through each ministry's spending and ministers announce new schemes.
Government Parliamentary Committee: the governing party's backbench MPs who shadow one ministry.
An MP with no government job.
The seats in Parliament where the ministers sit.
A new MP's first speech in Parliament.
The speech that opens each new term of Parliament, setting out the government's plans; Members then debate it.
Parliament's rule book; the Standing Orders Committee decides how the rules apply.
The party's local office and volunteers in an MP's ward.
The person, usually the governing party's MP, appointed to advise a ward's community groups.
The body, run by a ward's MPs, that maintains and manages the HDB estates in it.
Extra pay for ministers, from nothing up to six months' salary, tied to four national targets.
The President's official residence, where ministers are sworn in.
The Prime Minister's yearly speech to the nation in August, in several languages.
Member of Parliament.
The standing partnership of government, unions and employers, which settles wage guidelines together.
The law against online falsehoods: a minister can direct a post's author to attach a correction notice to it.
Central Provident Fund: the compulsory savings every worker pays into, for retirement, housing and health.
The Housing and Development Board: builds and sells the public flats most Singaporeans live in.
Build-To-Order: a new HDB flat, sold by ballot before it is built.
An HDB flat bought second-hand from its owner, at market price.
A newer HDB town far from the centre, with fewer amenities; its flats are cheaper.
HDB's three classes of new flat: Plus and Prime flats are more central and more subsidised, and owners must stay longer and repay more when they sell.
The open ground floor of an HDB block, used for meetings, chess, weddings and funerals.
Coffee, local style, from a coffee shop.
The national exam at the end of primary school, which decides secondary school places.
MediShield Life: the national basic health insurance scheme.
The national water agency.
The Singapore Tourism Board.
The Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore, the tax authority.
Service and conservancy charges: the monthly fee HDB residents pay their Town Council for the estate's upkeep.
Singapore's main English-language daily newspaper.
The Straits Times's letters page.
A Singapore online forum, known for its long, angry threads.
The statue of a lion's head on a fish's body at Marina Bay, Singapore's emblem for tourists.
